facts.claim: Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object from Earth, currently over 15 billion miles away.
Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977, 16 days after its twin Voyager 2.
Voyager 1 entered interstellar space on August 25, 2012, crossing the heliopause.
Voyager 1's velocity relative to the Sun is approximately 17 kilometers per second (38,000 mph).
Voyager 1 carries a Golden Record with sounds and images selected by a committee led by Carl Sagan.
Voyager 1's radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) produce about 238 watts of power, down from 470 watts at launch.
Voyager 1's signal takes about 22.5 hours to travel to Earth (one-way).
Voyager 1 discovered that the heliosphere protects the Solar System, and its instruments detected a constant density of plasma in interstellar space.
Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune.
The Voyager program is managed by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, with mission operations continuing as of 2026.
Voyager 1 is expected to continue transmitting data until around 2025, with all science instruments off by 2030 (but it is still transmitting as of early 2026).
Voyager 1's original primary mission was to explore Jupiter and Saturn, but it was extended to study the outer heliosphere.
The Voyager spacecraft were built with 3.7-meter diameter high-gain antennas, and their communication power is only about 20 watts.
Voyager 1 is exiting the Solar System in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus.
Voyager 1's position is tracked with an accuracy of a few meters using the Deep Space Network's radio telescopes.

hook_ideas: Start with a countdown: 'It’s been 48 years since a tiny probe left Earth, and it’s now 22 light-hours away.'
Show a live simulation of Voyager 1's position versus the Solar System's boundary.
Ask the audience: 'What does it mean to be the farthest human object? We haven't seen it, but we hear it.'
Play a snippet of the Golden Record sounds and ask: 'Who might hear this? No one—for billions of years.'
Use the detail that Voyager 1's signal is only 20 watts—like a refrigerator light—yet it's detectable from 15 billion miles away.
misconceptions: Voyager 1 has left the Solar System. In reality, it has entered interstellar space, but it is still within the Sun's gravitational influence (the Oort Cloud) which extends trillions of miles.
Voyager 1 is the fastest human-made object. That distinction belongs to the Parker Solar Probe during its perihelion, though Voyager 1 has the highest heliocentric velocity among distant probes.
Voyager 1 is powered by solar panels. It actually uses radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) fueled by plutonium-238, since sunlight is too weak at that distance.
Voyager 1's Golden Record carries only sounds and images for Earthlings. It's actually a message for any potential extraterrestrial civilization, with instructions in symbols.
